newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes little changed in U.S. before payrolls. [corrected 23:30 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes little changed in U.S. before payrolls. [corrected 23:30 gmt]

text.p: The dollar closed nearly flat after retreating from a new high versus the mark and failing to reclaim 112 yen before U.S. September Jobs data.

The dollar eked out a fresh 10-week high at 1.5341 marks before retreating early Thursday. But the dollar could get no traction above 112 yen -- where it set a 32-month high on Wednesday -- before the unemployment data, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday.
"It's just been a bit of profit taking going into the employment numbers," said Tim Summerfield, senior foreign exchange trader at Bank of Boston.
The dollar closed at 1.5298/08 marks, and 111.42/49 yen against 1.5301/04 marks and 111.40/45 yen at the open. (Corrects to show dollar was not up against the mark.)

Wall Street economists polled by Reuters predict that non-farm payrolls rose 166,000 in September, after increasing 250,000 in August. The unemployment rate is forecast to increase slightly to 5.2 percent from 5.1 percent.

The September numbers have a special importance since the Fed surprised the market by declining to tighten monetary policy in September, despite steamy 4.2 percent economic growth in the second quarter.

Traders are nervous that tight labor market conditions will produce higher inflation and force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates which might depress U.S. bonds and stocks and could unsettle the dollar in the short term if foreign investors then decide to pare holdings of U.S. assets.
But a weak number could help the dollar by increasing investor confidence that the Fed has inflation under control.

"If we get numbers that reaffirm the Fed's decision ..., then the market might actually buy dollars, as a sense of confidence in the Fed starts to pervade," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.

Meanwhile, the market still has an appetite to buy dollars amid consistently pro-dollar comments from several high- profile G7 officials following the gathering of finance ministers and central bankers over the weekend in Washington.

The latest comment was by French President Jacques Chirac, who said in a French magazine interview to appear on Saturday that the dollar is really undervalued and coordination between the Fed and other big central banks to ensure its proper value should be enhanced.

His comments followed remarks by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who said in a speech at the Economic Club of New York on Wednesday that he believed the U.S. has the economic potential and the credibility to maintain a strong dollar, as well as the political will to do so.

"There is no doubt that all the officials coming out of this past weekend's G7 meetings are hitting the pavement with the same talk -- 'strong dollar'," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole. "It is doing a lot to keep the dollar at these higher levels."
Traders said dollar/yen was well supported by buying interest between 111.20 and 111.40 but capped by sell orders and rumors the Bank of Japan was quietly taking profits above 112 overnight.
Large offers were reported in dollar/mark at 1.5330.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2554/61 Swiss from 1.2525/30 at the open and it fell to Canadian $1.3600/05 from C$1.3608/03. The pound slipped to $1.5652/59 from $1.5655/65.
The Australian dollar fell to $0.7909/14 from $0.7944/49.
